recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Bio: Kyle Denton is a community herbalist and medicine maker from Wisconsin who founded Tippecanoe Herbs with his wife Serena Marinelli in 2015. From their Milwaukee apothecary they craft small batch remedies from locally harvested and organic herbs, working from a bio terrain philosophy that blends Ayurveda with Western herbalism. He also runs Root Radical Herbal Academy, has taught for over a decade through his annual three season class and his Milwaukee herb walks, and sees clients as the Tuning Herbalist, using tuning forks to read the biofield. His Substack and podcast, Resonature, explore the interval between vital herbalism, biofield tuning and cosmology.
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Name: Kyle Denton
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Role: Community herbalist, founder of Tippecanoe Herbs

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Nature Is Alive", "body": "Matthew Wood traces his whole path back to a Quaker childhood, tenth generation, and a first day school teacher named Francis Hole, a soil science professor from Madison who took the children up Rib Mountain near Wausau, Wisconsin and radiated one conviction: nature is alive. Wood says he knew instantly it was true, and draws from it a shamanic rule he has kept since, that you must honor a revelation from the spirit or you will not be gifted that way again. Visiting Hole decades later, he was told he had chosen his profession well, because people crave to know nature is alive and cannot find the way there."}, {"title": "What the Word Medicine Actually Means", "body": "Pressed by Chance Garton for a definition broader than the allopathic one, Wood explains that for American Indian people medicine cannot be practiced without an inspiration, a vision or a dream, and that elder councils at the green corn dance would weigh the dreams of young people for what they meant and how they served the community. Medicine, he says, can be a plant, a dream, a song or a story, anything that heals or changes for the benefit of a person or society. He tracks the word into English through Grinnell, Brad Steiger, and Sun Bear and Wabun. Kyle Denton reframes it as a verb."}, {"title": "The Green Language, Phossus and Logos", "body": "Garton, whose stated interest is philology, mythology and symbolism, floats the idea that leaves and the shapes of plants may have been the very first form of writing. Wood answers that animals belong in there too, noting the Phoenician alphabet carried ox and snake alongside doorway and field, and calls plants and animals the primal shamanic alphabet. He credits the term green tongue to the esoteric writer David Ova's son, and says his late friend Robert Schmidt drew out the split between phossus, exact description, and logos, the syllogism Aristotle credits to Plato. Wood names Heraclitus the Dark and Jesus as the only ruthlessly phossic speakers he has found."}, {"title": "Plant Journeying and Trusting Intuition", "body": "Wood dates the flowering of plant journeying to the last thirty years or so, pointing back to Rudolf Steiner's advice that if you cannot find a teacher on the outer plane you should tune into plants, to Steiner's herbalist friend Leo Kugowski riding the commuter train into Vienna, and to Dr. Bach in the 1930s, whose society later refused any addition to his canon. Denton describes the mystery tea he learned from Jim MacDonald and Linda Conroy, where students smell an unnamed plant and report impressions before he names it and reads Wood's Earthwise Herbal back to them."}, {"title": "The Animal Self and Deserving to Know", "body": "Reading from Shamanic Herbal, Garton calls Wood's line his favorite definition of a shaman he has heard: anyone of any culture who experiences their animal self as a being as complete and important as their human self, which is why the universal symbol is the half animal, half human ideogram. Garton also relays Wood's two kinds of wisdom, one from living a good hearted life and one from learning nature's underlying patterns. Wood contrasts Native teaching, where an answer arrives as an analogous story you must deserve to decode, with no child left behind. Denton reads echinacea's spines as Pisces, pickiness and wanting one's own space."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Matthew Wood is a master teacher of the plant path who has shown thousands the way to find their spiritual and herbal medicine through his institute and many books, including one of our favorite InnerVerse regulars, Kyle Denton of Tippecanoe Herbs, who joins us in this conversation to discuss the highest truth: nature is alive! In his new book "A Shamanic Herbal", Matthew Wood conveys the ancient and universal wisdom of shamanism, and in this episode we discuss "medicine powers," the green language, and how to learn from the plants themselves.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Four Pillars of Shamanic Healing", "body": "Matthew Wood shares a dream from late 2022 that revealed four pillars of shamanic healing he had never taught before: naming the archetype, measuring the vital force, securing commitment, and detoxification. He insists archetypes are fixed rather than Jungian and mutable, changing only across vast timescales, so a practitioner cannot let them drift mid-treatment. Kyle Denton connects the vital force pillar to his own biofield tuning work, where a tuning fork reads voltage around the body the way Matthew reads it through the pulse, both tracing energetic imprints back to the moment a pattern first formed."}, {"title": "Commitment as a Hidden Cause of Illness", "body": "The pillar Matthew had never consciously treated before is commitment, since patients are not equally committed to their own healing and the shortfall itself keeps them sick. He ranks the failures from mildest to worst: simple lack of energy, laziness as a fault of character, lack of inspiration, and addiction as the deepest rut. He and Kyle trade herbal remedies for each level, floating buddleja for a lack of inspiration and saffron for the same, while noting men in particular tend to abandon herbal directions faster than women once a case leaves the clinic."}, {"title": "The Three Selves and the Making of a Shaman", "body": "Matthew lays out three selves that make up a person: the human self, seated in the heart's vulnerability; the animal self, felt from the neck down and only fully actualized through a dream of one's medicine animal; and a spirit or familiar self that walks ahead of a person. He describes his own dreams of a wolf and a turtle rising up his spine like a slower, more reliable path than the snake's, and calls the moment a medicine animal is dreamed into being the actual threshold of becoming a shaman, a lifetime achievement Don Juan tells Castaneda most people only reach once."}, {"title": "Fairies as the Tumblers of Creation", "body": "Matthew describes fairies as inorganic beings without an animal or human self, pure spirit that both craves human souls and is craved in return, which is why their world is dangerous to commit to. In a 2022 dream, and independently in a friend's dream the same period, the fairies offered their medicines freely instead of demanding payment, which he reads as a shift in how creation is willing to help people right now. He and Kyle connect the word fairy to furriness, landing on mullein, whose furred leaves and rocket-straight growth make it, in his words, an exceptional plant tied to sacred timing."}, {"title": "Pineal Calcification and Spiritual Blinding", "body": "Toward the end of the exclusive conversation, Matthew reframes third eye calcification some people report after covid vaccination as a vital response rather than a direct chemical injury, the body voluntarily narrowing spiritual perception the way blinders keep a spooked horse from breaking its leg. He describes calcite building up on the pineal gland much like the calcium phosphate rings that mark its age each year, and shares a formula of mullein, white pine, and teasel for clearing it, alongside shilajit, called the destroyer of weakness in Tibet, and holly for the irrational hatred he felt covid directing at him personally."}]
